prose_changes.old: Shaped by Lutheran and Reformed influences taking root in England, and the parent of both the Anglican tradition and the dissenting Protestant churches that broke from it. Its story extends through the Stuart century, from the 1604 Hampton Court Conference to the Westminster Assembly.
prose_changes.new: Shaped by Lutheran and Reformed influences taking root in England. It carried on as the Church of England, and its Puritan wing gave rise to the churches that later broke away. Its story runs through the Stuart century, from the Hampton Court Conference of 1604 to the Westminster Assembly.
prose_changes.reason: 'Parent of the Anglican tradition' becomes the continuation into the Restoration church (the 1662 Act cites the Elizabethan book). The dissenting churches came out of its Puritan wing (Baxter; Smyth, with McGlothlin), so the sentence routes them through Puritanism. The long first sentence is split and the last lightly reworded for reading level.

prose_changes.old: It became the Church of England, and through it the worldwide Anglican Communion. Its most far-reaching bequest is verbal: the cadences of the Book of Common Prayer and of the King James Bible of 1611 shaped English-language worship, and phrases from both — 'till death us do part', 'ashes to ashes, dust to dust' — passed into ordinary speech far beyond any church. The dissenting traditions that later broke away from it, Puritan, Congregational and Baptist, are equally its children.
prose_changes.new: It became the Church of England, and through it the worldwide Anglican Communion. Its most far-reaching gift is in words. The rhythms of the Book of Common Prayer and of the King James Bible of 1611 shaped worship in English. Phrases from both, like 'till death us do part' and 'ashes to ashes, dust to dust', passed into everyday speech far beyond any church. Puritanism grew up inside it. The Congregational, Presbyterian and Baptist churches that later stood outside it grew out of that Puritan wing.
prose_changes.reason: Puritanism did not break away as a church: its ministers were ejected in 1662, and the Baptists had left earlier. The sources show both lines coming from Puritan ministers, so the last sentence says so. The middle sentences are split for reading level; their content is unchanged.

prose_changes.old: Child of Geneva; distinct national-covenantal formation logic (a real uniqueness test)
prose_changes.new: Shaped by Geneva, whose order of worship its Assembly took up in 1562. What set it apart was national: a whole people bound to God by a public oath.
prose_changes.reason: 'Child of Geneva' claims descent; the sources show influence (the General Assembly's act of December 1562 and the Geneva service book). '(a real uniqueness test)' was build commentary inside a live field and is removed. The fragment becomes two sentences.

prose_changes.old: Grew directly out of Calvin's Geneva, and became one of history's clearest examples of a persecuted community scattering into exile across an entire continent.
prose_changes.new: Grew out of Calvin's Geneva, which wrote its creed and sent it pastors. Hunted at home, its people later fled across Europe and beyond, in one of history's clearest cases of a church driven into exile.
prose_changes.reason: 'Directly' outruns the evidence; French Protestant roots older than Geneva are not in these texts. The clause now names what the sources show: Calvin's draft of the confession and a pastor sent from Geneva. The long sentence is split for reading level.

prose_changes.old: Child of Geneva + the English settlement's tensions; parent of the evangelical line
prose_changes.new: Shaped by Geneva and grown inside the English church, which it thought only half reformed. Its stress on a personal turn to God later fed the revival in New England.
prose_changes.reason: 'Child of Geneva' becomes influence (Beza's and Gualter's letters printed with the Admonition); 'parent of the evangelical line' becomes influence (Edwards quoting Shepard), seventy years on. The fragment with '+' is rewritten as plain sentences.

prose_changes.old: Puritanism did not survive as a church of its own, but it left more behind than most movements that did. English Congregationalism, Presbyterianism and much of the Baptist tradition come straight out of it, and so does the culture of early New England, including Harvard, founded in 1636 to train its ministers. Its books stayed in print — Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, written by a man formed in that tradition, became one of the most widely read books in English. And its insistence on personal conversion runs directly into the evangelical revivals of the following century.
prose_changes.new: Puritanism did not survive as a church of its own, but it left more behind than most that did. English Congregationalism, Presbyterianism and much of the Baptist tradition came straight out of it. So did the culture of early New England, including Harvard, founded in 1636 to train its ministers. Its books stayed in print. Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, by a man formed in that tradition, became one of the most read books in English. And its call to a personal turn to God fed the revivals of the next century: in New England, Jonathan Edwards still quoted the Puritan Thomas Shepard.
prose_changes.reason: 'Runs directly into' claimed more than the evidence; the source shows Edwards quoting Shepard in 1746, and the sentence now names that tie. Other sentences are lightly shortened for reading level; their content is unchanged.
